newsitem.title: SPAIN: SWIMMING-INTERNATIONAL CALENDAR BECOMES MORE CROWDED.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-INTERNATIONAL CALENDAR BECOMES MORE CROWDED.

text.p: European swimming's governing body decided on Monday to intensify its championship programme, swelling an already crowded international calendar.
The European Swimming League (LEN) decided it would stage its short-course (25-metre pool) championships, first held last December, every year from 1998.
The LEN extraordinary congress also changed the year sequence for the biennial European long-course (50-metre pool) championships to avoid a clash with the world long-course championships.
The European long-course championships, first staged in 1926 and held every two years since 1981, will take place in both 1999 and 2000 and in even-numbered years from then on.

World swimming's governing body (FINA) decided in April to stage its global long-course championships every two years instead of every four, moving to odd-numbered years in 2001 after the next edition in Perth in January 1998.
FINA also holds world short-course championships every two years.
The aim of both FINA and LEN is to increase the profile and marketing potential of a sport generally rated second only to athletics at the Olympic Games.
Critics say it makes excessive demands on swimmers, who additionally face an expanding series of World Cup meetings between January and March.

In the Olympic year of 2000, for example, they could compete in five major international competitions -- World Cup (currently January-March), world short-course championships (April) , European long-course championships (June/July), Olympic Games ( September) and European short-course championships (December).
The LEN congress also agreed to expand the European long-course championship programme by adding 50-metre races in backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly from the next edition in Istanbul in 1999.
